'''3I/ATLAS''', also known as '''C/2025 N1 (ATLAS)''' and previously as '''A11pl3Z''',<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sparkes |first=Matthew |date=2 July 2025 |title=Interstellar comet hurtling through solar system named 3I/ATLAS |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/2486670-interstellar-comet-hurtling-through-solar-system-named-3i-atlas/ |access-date=13 February 2026 |website=New Scientist |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Baker |first=Harry |date=3 July 2025 |title=NASA confirms that mysterious object shooting through the solar system is an 'interstellar visitor' — and it has a new name |url=https://www.livescience.com/space/comets/nasa-confirms-that-mysterious-object-shooting-through-the-solar-system-is-an-interstellar-visitor-and-it-has-a-new-name |access-date=13 February 2026 |website=Live Science |language=en}}</ref> is an [[interstellar comet]]<ref name="NASA-Hubble-Aug2025"/><ref name="ESA-Hubble-Aug2025"/> discovered on 1 July 2025 by the [[Asteroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System]] (ATLAS) station. The comet follows an unbound, [[hyperbolic trajectory]] past the Sun,<ref name=vinf-perihelion/>{{efn|name=vinf-formula}} and passed by Earth at 1.8 [[AU (astronomy)|AU]], posing no threat.<ref name="NASA-FAQ"/> The prefix "3I" designates it as the third confirmed interstellar object passing through the [[Solar System]], after [[1I/{{okina}}Oumuamua]] and [[2I/Borisov]].<ref name="UT-20250702"/>

3I/ATLAS is an active comet consisting of a solid icy [[Comet nucleus|nucleus]] and a [[Coma (comet)|coma]], which is a cloud of gas and [[Comet dust|icy dust]] escaping from the nucleus. The Sun is responsible for the comet's activity because it heats up the comet's nucleus to [[Sublimation (phase transition)|sublimate]] its ice into gas, which [[Outgassing|outgasses]] and lifts up dust from the comet's surface to form its coma.<ref name="SciAm-20250717"/> Images taken by the [[Hubble Space Telescope]] and various [[interplanetary spacecraft]] suggest that the diameter of 3I/ATLAS's nucleus is less than {{cvt|1|km|mi}}.<ref name="Jewitt2025"/><ref name="Eubanks2025-nongravs"/> Observations by the [[James Webb Space Telescope]] (JWST) have shown that 3I/ATLAS is unusually rich in [[carbon dioxide]], and contains a small amount of [[Ice|water ice]], [[water vapor]], [[carbon monoxide]], [[carbonyl sulfide]], and [[methane]].<ref name="Cordiner2025"/><ref name="belyakov etal" /> Observations by the [[Very Large Telescope]] have also shown that 3I/ATLAS is emitting [[cyanide]] gas and atomic [[nickel]] vapor, at concentrations similar to those seen in Solar System comets.<ref name="Rahatgaonkar2025"/>

The comet came to [[solar conjunction]] on 21 October 2025,{{efn|name=SOT}} and it came [[perihelion|closest to the Sun]] on 29 October 2025, at a distance of {{convert|1.36|AU|e6km e6mi|abbr=unit}} from the Sun, which is between the orbits of Earth and [[Mars]].<ref name="jpldata"/> The comet appears to have originated from either the [[Milky Way]]'s [[thin disk]], or [[thick disk]];<ref name="Guo2025"/> if 3I/ATLAS originated from the thick disk, the comet could be at least 7 billion years old{{emdash}}older than the Solar System.<ref name="ras-July2025"/><ref name="Hopkins2025"/>

== History ==

=== Discovery ===

3I/ATLAS was discovered on 1 July 2025{{efn|In the [[Minor Planet Center]] discovery announcement, the discovery observation time (marked with an [[asterisk]] "*") is "2025 07 01.218880,"<ref name="MPEC-2025-N12"/> which translates to 1 July 2025 05:15:11 [[Universal Time|UT]].<ref name="horizons-discovery"/> While [[Precovery|earlier observations]] were later found, this was the first that was reported to the Minor Planet Center, received on 1 July 2025 at 07:48 UT.<ref name="MPCdesig"/>}} by the [[NASA]]-funded [[Asteroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System|ATLAS]] survey telescope at [[Río Hurtado]], Chile ([[List of observatory codes#W68|observatory code W68]]).<ref name="NASA-20250702"/><ref name="NYT-20250702"/><ref name="Bolin2025"/> At [[apparent magnitude]] 18, the newly discovered object was entering the inner Solar System at a speed of {{cvt|61|km/s|mph kph}} relative to the Sun,<ref name="NASA-FAQ"/> located {{convert|3.50|AU|e6km e6mi|abbr=unit|lk=in}} from Earth and {{val|4.51|u=AU}} from the Sun,<ref name="horizons-discovery"/> and was moving in the sky along the border of the [[constellation]]s [[Serpens Cauda]] and [[Sagittarius (constellation)|Sagittarius]], near the [[galactic plane]].<ref name="UT-20250702"/> It was given the temporary designation 'A11pl3Z' and the discovery observations were submitted to the [[International Astronomical Union]]'s [[Minor Planet Center]] (MPC).<ref name="MPCdesig"/><ref name="NYT-20250702"/> These observations initially suggested that the object could be on a highly [[orbital eccentricity|eccentric]] path that might come close to Earth's orbit, which led the MPC to temporarily list the object on the [[Near-Earth Object Confirmation Page]] until the orbit could be confirmed.<ref name="NYT-20250702"/>

Follow-up observations from other observatories, involving both professional and [[amateur astronomer]]s,<ref name="Conv-20250702"/> began to reveal that the object's trajectory would not come near Earth, but instead could be interstellar with a [[hyperbolic trajectory]].<ref name="NYT-20250702"/><ref name="EarthSky-2025"/> [[Precovery|Pre-discovery]] observations of 3I/ATLAS confirmed its interstellar trajectory; these included [[Zwicky Transient Facility]] (ZTF, observatory code [[List of observatory codes#I41|I41]]) observations from 28 to 29 June 2025 that were found within a few hours of the initial report,<ref name="MPCdesig"/> ZTF observations from 14 to 21 June 2025,<ref name="MPEC-2025-N12"/><ref name="IFLSci-20250702"/> and ATLAS observations from 25 to 29 June 2025.<ref name="UT-20250702"/><ref name="NYT-20250702"/><ref name="EarthSky-2025"/> Amateur astronomer Sam Deen has noted additional ATLAS pre-discovery observations from 5 to 25 June 2025, and suspected that 3I/ATLAS was not discovered earlier because it was passing in front of the [[Galactic Center]]'s dense star fields, where the comet would be hard to discern.<ref name="CBET5578"/>

Initial observations of 3I/ATLAS were unclear on whether it is an [[asteroid]] or a [[comet]].<ref name="UT-20250702"/><ref name="Conv-20250702"/><ref name="IFLSci-20250702"/> Various astronomers including [[Alan Hale (astronomer)|Alan Hale]] reported no cometary features,<ref name="CBET5578"/> but observations on 2 July 2025 by the Deep Random Survey ([[List of observatory codes#X09|X09]]) at Chile, [[Lowell Discovery Telescope]] ([[List of observatory codes#G37|G37]]) at [[Arizona]], and [[Canada–France–Hawaii Telescope]] ([[List of observatory codes#T14|T14]]) at [[Mauna Kea]] all showed a marginal [[Coma (comet)|coma]] with a potential tail-like elongation 3 [[arcsecond]]s in [[Angular distance|angular length]], which indicated the object is a comet.<ref name="MPEC-2025-N12"/><ref name="CBET5578"/> On 2 July 2025, the MPC announced the discovery of 3I/ATLAS and gave it the [[interstellar object#Nomenclature|interstellar object designation]] "3I", signifying it being the third interstellar object confirmed.<ref name="MPEC-2025-N12"/><ref name="CBET5578"/> The MPC also gave 3I/ATLAS the [[non-periodic comet]] designation C/2025 N1 (ATLAS).<ref name="MPEC-2025-N12"/> By the time 3I/ATLAS was officially named, the MPC had collected 122 observations of the comet from 31 different observatories.<ref name="MPEC-2025-N12"/>

=== Further observations ===
[[File:3I-ATLAS lightcurve Martinez-Palomera et al. 2025 Fig 4.png|thumb|upright=1.5|[[Light curve]] plot showing the measured brightness of 3I/ATLAS from May to August 2025, expressed in [[apparent magnitude]]. The brightness of 3I/ATLAS increases over time because it was approaching the Sun during this time interval. The gray shaded region represents the time when 3I/ATLAS was observed by the [[Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite]] (TESS).]]
[[File:Webb Images Combined 3I ATLAS.png|thumb|upright=1.5|3I/ATLAS imaged by the [[James Webb Space Telescope]]'s [[NIRSpec]] on 6 August 2025, showing an extended coma (left image). The two image panels on the right show how the brightness of 3I/ATLAS's coma changes depending on the [[wavelength]] of light, due to [[Emission spectrum|infrared light emission]] from the [[Rotational–vibrational spectroscopy|rotation and vibration of gas molecules]] in the coma.<ref name="Cordiner2025"/> The middle image shows [[carbon dioxide]] emission and the right image shows [[water vapor]] emission in 3I/ATLAS.]]
Observations by [[David C. Jewitt]] and [[Jane Luu]] using the [[Nordic Optical Telescope]] on 2 July 2025 confirmed that 3I/ATLAS was "clearly active" with a diffuse appearance.<ref name="ATel-17263"/> Miguel R. Alarcón and a team of researchers of the IAC ([[Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias]]) using [[Teide Observatory]]'s Two-meter Twin Telescope also found cometary activity on the same date.<ref name="ATel-17264"/> Multiple different telescopes showed that the comet's coma had a reddish color indicative of dust, similar to that of the previous interstellar comet 2I/Borisov.<ref name="Seligman2025"/><ref name="Bolin2025"/><ref name="Santana-Ros2025"/> A study published by Toni Santana-Ros and colleagues in August 2025 reported that 3I/ATLAS's coma had become redder throughout July 2025, indicating an evolving surface or coma composition as a result of 3I/ATLAS's increasing cometary activity.<ref name="Santana-Ros2025"/>{{rp|2}}

On 6 July, additional observations were published, including [[Zwicky Transient Facility]] (I41) [[precoveries]] from several nights between 22 May and 21 June 2025.<ref name="MPEC 2025-N51"/> An even earlier precovery from 21 May 2025, made at [[List of observatory codes#M01|Weizmann Astrophysical Observatory]] (M01), was published on 18 July 2025.<ref name="MPEC 2025-O20"/>

[[Polarimetry|Polarimetric]] observations by the [[Very Large Telescope]], Nordic Optical Telescope, and [[Rozhen Observatory]] from July and August 2025 revealed that 3I/ATLAS's coma exhibits an unusually high degree of negative [[Polarization (waves)|polarization]] at small [[phase angle (astronomy)|phase angles]]—meaning a large percent of the light reflected from 3I/ATLAS's coma have their oscillations oriented along the Sun-comet-observer plane.<ref name="Gray2025"/>{{rp|2}} The negative polarization of 3I/ATLAS appears similar to those seen in [[trans-Neptunian object]]s, and suggests that its coma is made of a mixture of icy and dark material.<ref name="Gray2025"/>{{rp|6–7}}

The newly commissioned [[Vera C. Rubin Observatory]] has serendipitously imaged 3I/ATLAS during its science validation observations from 21 June to 3 July 2025.<ref name="Chandler2025"/> These observations showed a slight increase in the comet's coma diameter and provided constraints on the comet's nucleus diameter.<ref name="Chandler2025"/> The Vera Rubin Observatory would have discovered 3I/ATLAS before the ATLAS survey if it had begun its science validation observations two weeks earlier.<ref name="Chandler2025"/>{{rp|26}} Rubin continued observing 3I/ATLAS until 20 July 2025, when the comet was no longer observable from Chile while the Sun was below the horizon; the observatory's 3200-megapixel [[Vera C. Rubin Observatory#LSSTCam|LSST Camera]] collected nearly 100 exposures across this period, capturing the comet's nightly evolution as it approached the Sun.<ref name="iotw2606a"/> NASA's [[Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite]] (TESS) had also observed 3I/ATLAS before it was discovered, with observations from 7 May to 3 June 2025.<ref name="Feinstein2025"/> These observations showed that the comet was already bright and active even when it was roughly 6.4&nbsp;AU away from the Sun in May 2025, which indicates the comet's activity is likely caused by the sublimation of [[volatile (astrogeology)|volatile ices]] other than water.<ref name="Feinstein2025"/>

[[Ice|Water ice]] in 3I/ATLAS's coma was first reported on 20 July 2025, based on [[near-infrared]] [[spectroscopic]] observations by the [[Gemini Observatory|Gemini South]] and [[NASA Infrared Telescope Facility]] on 5 and 14 July 2025.<ref name="Yang2025"/> [[Ultraviolet]] observations by the [[Swift Observatory]] suggested the presence of [[water vapor]] and [[hydroxide]] [[ion]]s in 3I/ATLAS's coma on 30 July 2025 and 1 August 2025.<ref name="Xing2025"/> On 21 August 2025, astronomers of NASA's [[SPHEREx]] mission and the [[California Institute of Technology]] reported the detection of water ice and bright [[carbon dioxide]] gas emission in SPHEREx observations from mid-August 2025.<ref name="Lisse2025"/><ref name="SPHEREx"/> On 22 August 2025, astronomers at [[Lowell Observatory]] reported the first tentative detection of [[cyanide]] emission in 3I/ATLAS.<ref name="ATel-17352"/> Spectroscopic observations by the [[Very Large Telescope]] on 21 August 2025 confirmed the presence of cyanide and also detected [[nickel]] in 3I/ATLAS's coma.<ref name="Rahatgaonkar2025"/><ref name="Smithsonian-Aug2025"/>

The [[Hubble Space Telescope]] took its first images of 3I/ATLAS on 21 July 2025, which revealed its coma in high detail and constrained its nucleus diameter to below {{cvt|5.6|km|mi}}.<ref name="HST_17830"/><ref name="Jewitt2025"/> The Hubble images were publicized by [[NASA]] and the [[European Space Agency]] on 7 August 2025.<ref name="NASA-Hubble-Aug2025"/><ref name="ESA-Hubble-Aug2025"/> On 6 August 2025, JWST made its first observations of 3I/ATLAS using its [[NIRSpec]] instrument,<ref name="JWST-schedule-2025Aug04"/><ref name="JWST5094"/> and results were announced by NASA on 25 August 2025.<ref name="NASA-JWST-Aug2025"/> In November 2025, Hubble performed [[ultraviolet]] spectroscopy on 3I/ATLAS to determine the composition of its gas emissions and [[sulfur]]-to-[[oxygen]] ratio,<ref name="SciAm-20250717"/><ref name="HST_17780"/> and the telescope will monitor the comet on its way out of the Solar System.<ref name="HST_18152"/> The JWST had made a second set of observations of 3I/ATLAS in December 2025, after the comet's perihelion.<ref name="SciAm-20250717"/><ref name="JWST9442"/><ref name="belyakov etal">{{cite journal |last1=Belyakov |first1=Matthew |last2=Wong |first2=Ian |last3=Bolin |first3=Bryce T. |last4=Davis |first4=M. Ryleigh |last5=Bromley |first5=Steven J. |last6=Lisse |first6=Carey M. |last7=Brown |first7=Michael E. |date=29 January 2026 |title=The Volatile Inventory of 3I/ATLAS as Seen with JWST/MIRI |journal=[[The Astrophysical Journal Letters]] |volume=1001 |issue=1 |pages=L11 |arxiv=2601.22034 |bibcode=2026ApJ..1001L..11B |doi=10.3847/2041-8213/ae5700 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

The comet was observed by the [[James Clerk Maxwell Telescope]] on 7 September 2025, when 3I/ATLAS was located 2.33 AU from the Sun, and found a [[hydrogen cyanide]] production rate of {{val|1.5|0.5|e=25}} molecules per second, while a week later, on September 14, the production rate had climbed to {{val|4.5|1.9|e=25}} molecules per second (2&nbsp;kg/s).<ref name="CBET5608">{{cite journal |last1=Green |first1=Daniel W. E. |title=COMET 3I/ATLAS |journal=Central Bureau Electronic Telegrams |date=18 September 2025 |issue=5608 |url=http://www.cbat.eps.harvard.edu/iau/cbet/005600/CBET005608.txt |access-date=26 September 2025}}</ref> The cyanide coma on 15 September was about 180,000 kilometers across and was asymmetric, being elongated along the anti-solar direction. On the same date there was also a visible dust tail 50 arcseconds across, corresponding to about 100,000 kilometers.<ref name="ATel-17416"/> On 14 September, the comet had an [[apparent magnitude]] of 14.2.<ref name="CBET5608"/>

The [[Trace Gas Orbiter|ExoMars TGO]] with its Colour and Stereo Surface Imaging System (CaSSIS) imaged the coma of 3I/ATLAS as the comet made its closest approach to Mars.{{r|ESA20251007}} The comet was around 50,000 times fainter than what the orbiter is used to viewing and imaged using 5-second exposures.{{r|ESA20251007}}

== Trajectory ==
[[File:3I ATLAS animation3.gif|thumb|upright=1|Top view of 3I/ATLAS's trajectory (blue) through the Solar System, with orbits and positions of planets shown (click to start animation)]]
[[File:3I ATLAS animation2.webm|thumb|upright=1|Tilted view of 3I/ATLAS's trajectory through the Solar System, with orbits and positions of planets shown (click to start animation)]]
3I/ATLAS follows an extremely [[hyperbolic trajectory]] past the Sun because it is moving too fast to be bound by the Sun's gravity.<ref name="NASA-FAQ"/> When 3I/ATLAS entered the Solar System, it was moving at a speed of {{cvt|58|km/s|mi/s AU/month}} relative to the Sun {{Ndash}}this speed is the comet's [[hyperbolic excess velocity]] (''v''{{sub|∞}}).<ref name="Hopkins2025"/><ref name="Taylor2025"/>{{efn|name=vinf-formula|1=Formula for the [[Hyperbolic trajectory#Parameters describing a hyperbolic trajectory|hyperbolic excess velocity]]: <math>\sqrt{-GM/a}</math>, where <math>G</math> is the gravitational constant, <math>M</math> the mass of the Sun, and <math>a</math> the comet's semi-major axis. Calculation: [https://www.wolframalpha.com/input?i=sqrt%28-gravitational+constant+*+solar+mass+%2F+%28-0.26392+astronomical+units%29%29]}}<!-- Replace the number -0.26392 in the calculation with that from the most recent orbit.--> As 3I/ATLAS came closer to the Sun and was pulled in by the Sun's gravity, the comet sped up,<ref name="NASA-FAQ"/><ref name="Syfy-20250710"/> and then once it began moving away, the comet slowed down as the Sun's gravity began pulling back on it.<ref name="vinf-perihelion"/> The comet will escape the Solar System nevertheless.<ref name="EarthSky-2025"/> 3I/ATLAS is moving far faster than the previous two [[interstellar object]]s [[1I/{{okina}}Oumuamua]] (''v''{{sub|∞}}{{=}}{{val|26|u=km/s}}) and [[2I/Borisov]] (''v''{{sub|∞}}{{=}}{{val|32|u=km/s}}).<ref name="Taylor2025"/>

The shape of 3I/ATLAS's trajectory is described by a parameter known as the [[orbital eccentricity]].<ref name="IFLSci-20250702"/> Whereas [[elliptical orbit]]s have an eccentricity less than 1, hyperbolic orbits have an eccentricity greater than 1. For 3I/ATLAS, its trajectory has an extremely high [[orbital eccentricity]] of {{val|6.141|0.00002}}.<ref name="jpldata"/>{{efn|name=sigma}} This extremely high eccentricity makes the trajectory of 3I/ATLAS appear relatively straight, rather than curved.<ref name="LiveScience-20250710"/> 3I/ATLAS has the highest eccentricity of the three interstellar objects known to date,<ref name="Conv-20250702"/> greater than 1I/{{okina}}Oumuamua's (''e''=1.2) and 2I/Borisov's (''e''=3.4).<ref name="IFLSci-20250702"/>

3I/ATLAS passed closest to the Sun on 29 October 2025 at 11:45 UT.{{r|perihelion}}{{efn|name=n-body}} The comet's [[perihelion]] or closest distance to the Sun was {{convert|1.36|AU|e6km e6mi|lk=in|abbr=unit}}, which lies between the orbits of Earth and [[Mars]].<ref name="jpldata"/><ref name="NASA-FAQ"/> At perihelion, the comet was moving at its maximum speed of {{cvt|68|km/s|mi/s}} with respect to the Sun.<ref name="EarthSky-2025"/>{{efn|The escape velocity from the Solar System depends mostly on how close you are to the Sun. Mars at 1.5 AU from the Sun has an [[Orbital speed#Planets|orbital speed]] of only 24 km/s. The [[Escape velocity#List of escape velocities|escape velocity from the Solar System at Mercury's orbit]] at 0.4 AU from the Sun is about 68 km/s, which is 3I/ATLAS's velocity at 1.36 AU from the Sun. The escape velocity from the surface of the Sun is 618 km/s.}}

The trajectory of 3I/ATLAS is coincidentally closely aligned with the [[orbital plane]]s of the Solar System's planets, or the [[ecliptic]].<ref name="S&T-20250728"/><ref name="Plait-Jul2025"/> Specifically, the comet's trajectory is [[orbital inclination|tilted]] 175° ([[Retrograde and prograde motion|retrograde]] and inclined 5°) with respect to the ecliptic.<ref name="Seligman2025"/><ref name="jpldata"/> The trajectory of 3I/ATLAS brought the comet close to the planets [[Venus]], Mars, and [[Jupiter]], but not Earth,<ref name="S&T-20250728"/> and hence posed no threat.<ref name="NASA-FAQ"/><ref name="S&T-20250728"/><ref name="LiveScience-20250710"/> As 3I/ATLAS approached perihelion, it passed by Mars at a distance of {{convert|0.194|AU|e6km e6mi|abbr=unit}} on 3 October 2025.<ref name="horizons-Mars"/> After perihelion, it passed {{convert|0.65|AU|e6km e6mi|abbr=unit}} from Venus on 3 November 2025.<ref name="horizons-Venus"/> It passed {{convert|1.798|AU|e6km e6mi|abbr=unit}} from Earth on 19 December 2025,<ref name=Earth/>{{efn|name=Earth}} when it was inside the [[asteroid belt]] and beyond the 4:1 [[Kirkwood gap]].<ref name=Earth/>{{efn|name=Kirkwood|On 19 December 2025 the comet was 2.29 AU from the Sun and the [[Kirkwood gap#Main gaps|4:1 Kirkwood gap]] is located at 2.07 AU from the Sun.}} The comet passed {{convert|0.358|AU|e6km e6mi|abbr=unit}} from Jupiter on 16 March 2026.<ref name="jpldata"/>{{efn|name=Jupiter-RNG_3sigma}} The comet will reach the inner [[Oort cloud]] (2000 AU from the Sun) around the year 2189,<ref name=vinf-perihelion/> and will reach the outer edge of the Oort cloud ({{val|100000}}+ AU from the Sun) in about 8000 years.{{efn|name=Exit|At 12.24 AU/year, it will take about 8137 years to exit the Solar System. Math: 100 000 / (58 km/s * 60 seconds * 60 minutes * 24 hours * 365.25 days / AU)}}

== Observability ==
3I/ATLAS is a faint comet that does not get very close to Earth or the Sun and was not expected to get brighter than about [[apparent magnitude]] 11.5 as seen from Earth.<ref name="Yoshida"/><ref name="cobs"/> Even at its peak brightness, the comet was not visible to an observer on Earth using the [[naked eye]]<ref name="SETI"/> or smaller [[binoculars]].<ref name="binoculars">{{cite web |date=2004 |title=Limiting Magnitude in Binoculars |publisher=Cloudy Nights |first=Ed |last=Zarenski |url=http://www.cloudynights.com/documents/limiting.pdf |access-date=6 July 2025 |archive-date=21 July 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110721072103/http://www.cloudynights.com/documents/limiting.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>  3I/ATLAS has been imaged by [[astrometric solving|plate-solving]] [[Robotic telescope#Smart telescopes|smart telescopes]] with an [[aperture]] diameter of at least {{cvt|3 to 4.5|in|cm}} that see objects much fainter than visual observers do.<ref name="SETI"/> During the Mars approach on 3 October 2025, 3I/ATLAS had a total magnitude (nucleus+coma) of 12 which made it about 120 times fainter than comet [[C/2025 A6 (Lemmon)]] and about 190 times fainter than comet [[C/2025 R2 (SWAN)]] at the time.<ref name="cobs"/> By mid-November, the comet was on the borderline (between magnitudes 10 and 9) to be able to be detected in tripod-mounted 20x80 binoculars.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2025/nov/19/nasa-interstellar-comet-pictures|title=Nasa releases close-up pictures of comet flying by from another star system|agency=Associated Press|date=20 November 2025|work=The Guardian}}</ref>

From July to late September 2025, 3I/ATLAS was observable from Earth after sunset.<ref name="TheSkyLive"/> During the first half of July 2025, 3I/ATLAS was located in the [[constellation]] [[Sagittarius (constellation)|Sagittarius]] at an apparent magnitude of 17.5.<ref name="TheSkyLive"/> By the second half of July 2025, 3I/ATLAS had moved to the constellation [[Ophiuchus]] and had brightened to apparent magnitude 16.<ref name="TheSkyLive"/> During that time, the comet was located in a region of the sky where it was densely filled with stars, which made observations challenging as the comet could overlap background stars.<ref name="TheSkyLive"/> The comet continued brightening as it approached the Sun, and throughout August 2025 it moved across the constellations Ophiuchus, [[Scorpius (constellation)|Scorpius]], and [[Libra (constellation)|Libra]].<ref name="TheSkyLive"/> During September 2025, 3I/ATLAS remained in the constellation Libra as it brightens to around apparent magnitude 12–13.<ref name="TheSkyLive"/><ref name="cobs"/> Even under a dark sky, to visually observe a point-like star (much less a [[Surface brightness|diffuse]] comet) of magnitude 14 would require a telescope with an aperture of at least {{convert|200|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}},<ref name="limiting-magnitude"/> but given the diffuse nature of the object, a {{convert|300|mm|in|abbr=on}} telescope might be needed.{{efn|name=Telescope|For example, comet [[240P/NEAT]] at [https://web.archive.org/web/20250904045603/https://cometchasing.skyhound.com/index.html#Observing%20Synopses magnitude 13.9] required a 12-inch telescope to observe under a dark sky.}}

As the comet approached the 29 October 2025 perihelion passage, the comet's [[solar elongation]] or [[angular separation]] from the Sun in the sky continued to decrease, which narrowed down its visibility to only equatorial regions of Earth just after sunset.<ref name="TheSkyLive"/> The comet was less than 30 degrees from the Sun from 1 October 2025 to 9 November 2025.<ref name=solar-elongation/> The reason for 3I/ATLAS's decreasing solar elongation before perihelion is because the comet came to [[solar conjunction]] (on the opposite side of the Sun from Earth) on 21 October 2025,{{efn|name=SOT}} 8 days before perihelion.<ref name="UT-20250702"/><ref name="TheSkyLive"/> This means 3I/ATLAS appeared behind the Sun{{efn|name=SOT|1=The minimum angular separation between the Sun and 3I/ATLAS was [https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/horizons_batch.cgi?batch=1&COMMAND=%273I%27&START_TIME=%272025-10-21%2005:10%27&STOP_TIME=%272025-10-21%2006:10%27&STEP_SIZE=%2710%20min%27&QUANTITIES=%2723%27 2.59 degrees] on 21 October 2025 when the comet was 2.4 AU from Earth.}} from Earth during the comet's perihelion, so the comet was not observable from Earth during this time.<ref name="TheSkyLive"/><ref name="S&T-20250728"/> The comet passed close to Mars during that month and [[Mars orbiter]]s may be able to observe the comet near perihelion.<ref name="UT-20250702"/> The faint comet was observable from 18 to 24 October with the [[GOES-19]] weather satellite that can see objects down to magnitude 12.<ref name=Boonplod>[https://groups.io/g/comets-ml/message/34189 Worachate Boonplod on Comets-ML]</ref> During the same period it was also observed by [[Solar and Heliospheric Observatory]] and the [[Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere]] satellites.<ref name=Dickinson>{{cite news |last=Dickinson |first=David |date=28 October 2025 |title=Spying Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS Near Perihelion |url=https://www.universetoday.com/articles/spying-interstellar-comet-3iatlas-near-perihelion |work=Universe Today  |publisher=Universe Today  |access-date=29 October 2025}}</ref>

After 3I/ATLAS passed perihelion, it became visible in the sky again just before sunrise in November 2025.<ref name="TheSkyLive"/> Further observations and spectrometry was conducted by [[Physical Research Laboratory]] scientists from the [[Mount Abu InfraRed Observatory|1.2m infra-red telescope]] on [[Mount Abu]] in mid-November 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Observations of the Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS with the PRL 1.2m telescope at Mount Abu |url=https://www.isro.gov.in/Observations_Interstellar_Comet.html |access-date=19 November 2025 |website=www.isro.gov.in}}</ref> The comet grew dimmer and its solar elongation increased as it moved away from the Sun.<ref name="TheSkyLive"/> During December 2025, the comet will move through the constellations [[Virgo (constellation)|Virgo]] and [[Leo (constellation)|Leo]] and its brightness is expected to become dimmer than apparent magnitude 12.<ref name="TheSkyLive"/>

On 11 December 2025, the comet passed less than two degrees from the half Moon. By 11 December 2025, the comet went more than 90 degrees from the Sun and became observable at midnight.<ref name=SOT>[https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/horizons_batch.cgi?batch=1&COMMAND=%273I%27&START_TIME=%272025-12-11%2013:09%27&STOP_TIME=%272026-01-24%27&STEP_SIZE=%271%20d%27&QUANTITIES=%2719,23,20%27 December solar elongation (S-O-T)]</ref> But [[Opposition (astronomy)|opposition]], when the comet was up all night at an elongation of 177.6 degrees, did not occur until 22 January 2026, when the comet was predicted to be much fainter.<ref name=SOT/>

[[File:3I-ATLAS-starchart.svg|thumb|upright=3|center|The apparent path of 3I/ATLAS in Earth's sky from 2024 to 2026. The comet's positions over 10-day intervals are marked with red points and are labeled with their respective dates in yellow. The path begins in the [[constellation]] [[Sagittarius (constellation)|Sagittarius]] on the left and ends in [[Gemini (constellation)|Gemini]] on the right. The apparent loops at the path's ends are caused by [[parallax]] due to Earth's orbital motion around the Sun.]]

== Origin and age ==
{{multiple image
| direction         = vertical
| align             = right
| total_width       = 300
| image1            = 3I-ATLAS Milky Way orbit.png
| image2            = 3I-ATLAS Milky Way orbit side view.png
| footer            = Diagrams illustrating the orbits of the Sun (yellow) and 3I/ATLAS (red) within the [[Milky Way]] galaxy. 3I/ATLAS has a tilted orbit that brings it farther above and below the [[galactic plane]] than the Sun, as shown by the side view (bottom image).
}}

3I/ATLAS is recognized as an [[interstellar object]] because of its extremely hyperbolic path and very high speed relative to the Solar System.<ref name="NASA-FAQ"/> 3I/ATLAS did not pass close enough to any of the Solar System's planets to have gained its speed, so it could not have originated from the Solar System.<ref name="dela_Fuente_Marcos_2025"/>{{rp|7}} Tracing the path of 3I/ATLAS in the sky shows that the comet originated from [[interstellar space]] in the direction of the constellation Sagittarius, near the [[Milky Way]]'s [[Galactic Center]].<ref name="dela_Fuente_Marcos_2025"/>{{rp|3}}<ref name="Seligman2025"/>{{rp|5}}

Unlike the previous two interstellar objects, 3I/ATLAS originated from the [[southern celestial hemisphere]] in a direction opposite to the [[solar apex]] in the north,<ref name="dela_Fuente_Marcos_2025"/>{{rp|3}} which is the direction of the Sun's movement relative to local stars.<ref name="Hopkins2025"/>{{rp|6}} The southern origin of 3I/ATLAS was unexpected because astronomers initially predicted that more interstellar objects should come from the solar apex, and that telescopes should have a more difficult time discovering southern-origin interstellar objects.<ref name="Hopkins2025"/>{{rp|6–7}} It is possible that either 3I/ATLAS is a rare discovery, or southern-origin interstellar objects may be more common than initially thought.<ref name="Hopkins2025"/>{{rp|7}}

The origin of 3I/ATLAS can be deduced by breaking down its hyperbolic excess velocity into [[Stellar kinematics#Space velocity|radial (''U''), transverse (''V''), and vertical (''W'') velocity components]] in the [[galactic coordinate system]].<ref name="Hopkins2025"/>{{efn|In the [[galactic coordinate system]], ''U'' positive toward the direction of the [[Galactic Center]], ''V'' positive toward the direction of [[Milky Way#Galactic rotation|galactic rotation]], and ''W'' positive toward the direction of the [[North Galactic Pole]].<ref name="Hopkins2025"/>{{rp|2}}<ref name="UVW"/>}} When 3I/ATLAS arrived to the Solar System, it was moving away from the Galactic Center with a velocity of ''U''{{=}}{{val|-51.0|u=km/s}} with respect to the Sun{{efn|The Sun is also moving away from the Galactic Center and thus has a negative ''U'' velocity component, although it is slower than that of 3I/ATLAS.<ref name="UVW"/>}} and was moving upward through the [[galactic plane]] with a velocity of ''W''{{=}}+{{val|18.5|u=km/s}} with respect to the Sun.<ref name="Hopkins2025"/>{{rp|2}} The vertical ''W'' velocity of 3I/ATLAS is quite high compared to those of nearby stars and other interstellar objects, which means that the comet follows a tilted orbit around the Milky Way and thus belongs to either the [[thin disk]] or [[thick disk]] populations.<ref name="Guo2025"/> The thick disk mainly consists of older stars whose compositions have [[metallicity|lower levels of heavy elements than the Sun]].<ref name="ras-July2025"/><ref name="Hopkins2025"/>{{rp|3}}

A July 2025 study led by Matthew Hopkins and collaborators estimated with 68 percent confidence that 3I/ATLAS is between 7.6 and 14 billion years old, based on the typical ages of stars in the thick disk.<ref name="ras-July2025"/><ref name="Hopkins2025"/>{{rp|4}} This means that 3I/ATLAS could be older than the Solar System (which is 4.6 billion years old) and may well be the oldest comet yet seen.<ref name="ras-July2025"/><ref name="Hopkins2025"/>{{rp|4}} An independent analysis by Aster Taylor and Darryl Seligman in July 2025 estimated that 3I/ATLAS should be 3 to 11 billion years old, in broad agreement with Hopkins et al.'s estimate.<ref name="SciAm-20250717"/><ref name="Taylor2025"/>

=== Parent star and formation ===
3I/ATLAS cannot be traced back to its original parent star because the comet has been traveling around the Milky Way for billions of years, which is enough time for it to be mixed around with other stars.<ref name="SciAm-20250717"/><ref name="Hopkins2025"/>{{rp|2}} It is likely that 3I/ATLAS's speed has undergone changes during its journey through interstellar space, via [[gravity assist]]s from close encounters with stars and [[nebula]]e.<ref name="NASA-Hubble-Aug2025"/> A September 2025 study by Yiyang Guo and collaborators found that 3I/ATLAS may have passed within {{convert|1|pc|ly|abbr=off|lk=on}} of 25 known stars in the past 10 million years.<ref name="Guo2025"/>

Although the parent star of 3I/ATLAS is unknown, the properties and environment of its parent star can be inferred from the comet's composition and dynamical membership in the [[Galactic disc|Galactic disk]].<ref name="SciAm-20250717"/> If it is a member of the thick disk, the parent star of 3I/ATLAS could be a low-[[metallicity]] star with a heavy element abundance of at least 40 percent of the Sun's.<ref name="Taylor2025"/>{{rp|5}} 3I/ATLAS is presumed to have formed within a [[protoplanetary disk]] of gas and [[cosmic dust|dust]], which surrounded the parent star when it was young.<ref name="Taylor2025"/>{{rp|1}}<ref name="Hopkins2025"/>{{rp|1}} Observations by JWST and SPHEREx have shown that 3I/ATLAS is rich in [[carbon dioxide]] ({{chem|CO|2}}),<ref name="BigThink-Aug2025"/> which suggests that it formed far from its parent star, beyond the {{chem|CO|2}} [[Frost line (astrophysics)|frost line]] where temperatures are cold enough for {{chem|CO|2}} to [[condensations|condense]] into solid.<ref name="Cordiner2025"/> At some point after its formation, 3I/ATLAS was gravitationally flung out of its parent star system, either by a close encounter with a [[giant planet]] or a star.<ref name="Taylor2025"/>{{rp|1}}<ref name="Hopkins2025"/>{{rp|1}}<ref name="SciAm-20250717"/>

== Physical characteristics ==
=== Cometary activity ===
==== Coma ====
[[File:3I-ATLAS surface brightness plot.png|thumb|upright=1.5|'''Left panel:''' 3I/ATLAS imaged by the [[Very Large Telescope]] on 4 July 2025, showing the comet's fuzzy appearance relative to background stars around it. The comet appears elongated toward the Sun due to its Sun-facing plume.<br />'''Right panel:''' The fuzzy appearance of 3I/ATLAS can be seen in its radial brightness profile, which plots the [[surface brightness]] in relation to radius. 3I/ATLAS's surface brightness extends to a greater radius compared to a background star of the same peak brightness, so the comet must have a [[coma (comet)|coma]].]]

3I/ATLAS appears distinctly fuzzier than stars in telescope images, which means that the solid body or [[comet nucleus|nucleus]] of 3I/ATLAS is surrounded by a [[coma (comet)|coma]],<ref name="Seligman2025"/>{{rp|5}}<ref name="Bolin2025"/>{{rp|3}}<ref name="Chandler2025"/>{{rp|20}} a cloud of gas and [[comet|icy dust]] ejected from the comet's [[outgassing]] surface.<ref name="SETI"/><ref name="SciAm-20250717"/> The Sun is responsible for the comet's activity because it heats up the comet's nucleus to [[sublimation (phase transition)|sublimate]] its [[volatile (astrogeology)|volatile ices]] into gas, which ejects dust from the comet's surface and escapes into space.<ref name="SETI"/><ref name="SciAm-20250717"/> Dust particles in the coma of 3I/ATLAS eventually trail away from the nucleus (with smaller particles blown away by [[solar radiation pressure]]), leading to the formation of a dust [[comet tail|tail]] behind the comet.<ref name="Chandler2025"/>{{rp|24}}

As 3I/ATLAS came closer to the Sun, it became more active as its volatile ices heated up more and began sublimating faster;<ref name="Seligman2025"/>{{rp|10}} this could potentially have led to outbursts, where the comet suddenly ejects a large amount of dust and brightens,<ref name="SciAm-20250717"/><ref name="MSU-July2025"/> or even fragmentation events, where the comet's nucleus breaks into pieces like what happened with the previous interstellar comet 2I/Borisov.<ref name="SciAm-20250717"/><ref name="S&T-20250728"/> {{As of|August 2025}}, observations had not detected any outbursts in 3I/ATLAS; its brightness and activity level appear to be steady.<ref name="Frincke2025"/> Observations by NASA's [[Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite]] (TESS) show that 3I/ATLAS may have been exhibiting cometary activity as early as 7 May 2025 (two months before its discovery), when it was roughly 6.4&nbsp;AU away from the Sun.<ref name="Feinstein2025"/>

The coma of 3I/ATLAS appears slightly [[ellipse|elliptical]] and spans up to {{cvt|26400 by 24700|km|mi}} in diameter (about twice the [[Earth radius#Derived quantities: diameter, circumference, arc-length, area, volume|diameter of Earth]]),{{efn|Earth's mean diameter (averaged between poles and equator) is roughly {{cvt|12756|km|mi}} (see [[Earth radius|mean radius of Earth]]). Multiplying that by 2 gives {{cvt|25512|km|mi}}.}} according to high-resolution images from the {{convert|10.4|m|ft|adj=on|sp=us}} [[Gran Telescopio Canarias]] on 2 July 2025.<ref name="dela_Fuente_Marcos_2025"/>{{rp|2}} Observations by NASA's SPHEREx mission from mid-August 2025 showed that 3I/ATLAS has a more extensive carbon dioxide gas coma that spans at least {{cvt|348000|km|mi}} in radius, although it is only visible in [[near-infrared]].<ref name="SPHEREx"/> Because the comet is far away from Earth, its coma appears small in the sky; observations from July 2025 have measured an [[angular diameter]] of about 2 [[arcsecond]]s for the most visible part of the coma (the coma's [[full width at half maximum]])<ref name="Seligman2025"/>{{rp|5}}<ref name="Opitom2025"/>{{rp|2}}<ref name="Bolin2025"/>{{rp|1}} and 10 arcseconds for the full extent of the coma.<ref name="dela_Fuente_Marcos_2025"/>{{rp|2}} As 3I/ATLAS approaches the Sun and becomes more active, the size and density of its coma continued to grow. Pre-discovery observations by the [[Vera C. Rubin Observatory]] showed that the diameter of 3I/ATLAS's coma had grown from {{cvt|13040|km|mi}} on 21 June 2025 to {{cvt|18760|km|mi}} on 2 July 2025.<ref name="Chandler2025"/>{{rp|28}}

Spectroscopic and imaging observations indicate that the coma of 3I/ATLAS has a reddish color and is mainly made of relatively large dust grains that are several [[micrometre|micrometer]]s (μm) in radius.<ref name="Yang2025"/>{{rp|6}}<ref name="Bolin2025"/>{{rp|4}} The reddish color of 3I/ATLAS is similar to the colors of [[D-type asteroid]]s, Solar System comets, and the interstellar comet 2I/Borisov, and is likely caused by [[irradiation|irradiated]] [[organic compound]]s such as [[tholin]]s in the comet's coma.<ref name="Puzia2025"/> Within the coma of 3I/ATLAS, small dust grains with {{val|1|u=um}} radii are ejected from the nucleus at fast speeds of {{val|22|u=m/s}}, whereas large dust grains with {{val|100|u=um}} radii are ejected at slower speeds of about {{val|2|u=m/s}}.<ref name="Jewitt2025"/>{{rp|7}} Based on the shape and brightness of 3I/ATLAS's coma in [[Hubble Space Telescope]] images from July 2025, it is estimated that the comet was ejecting {{cvt|6|kg|lb}} of small dust particles per second and {{cvt|60|kg|lb}} of large dust particles per second during that month.<ref name="Jewitt2025"/>{{rp|7, 10}} The dust ejection rate of 3I/ATLAS is similar to that of 2I/Borisov when it was approaching the Solar System,<ref name="Bolin2025"/>{{rp|4}} but it is lower than the typical rates for distant [[Jupiter-family comet]]s.<ref name="Santana-Ros2025"/>{{rp|3}}

The ESA with data from the JANUS and JUICE spacecraft shows that 3I has a distinct coma, although the spacecraft was 60 million kilometers away at its closest Jupiter approach on 16 March 2026. Along with the two tails; dust tail and [[ion tail]], this further backs up that 3I is an ordinary comet.<ref name="ESA20260402">{{cite web |date=2 April 2026 |title=Five things Juice has revealed about Comet 3I/ATLAS |url=https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/Juice/Five_things_Juice_has_revealed_about_Comet_3I_ATLAS |issue=[[ESA]]}}</ref>

==== Sun-facing plume ====
During July and August 2025, the coma of 3I/ATLAS appeared to be elongated westward in the sky—in a direction toward the Sun and toward the comet's direction of motion rather than away.<ref name="Opitom2025"/>{{rp|4}}<ref name="Chandler2025"/>{{rp|22, 24}}<ref name="Cordiner2025"/> This Sun-facing feature is not a tail (contrary to initial reports),<ref name="Santana-Ros2025"/><ref name="Jewitt2025"/>{{rp|5}} but is rather a dust plume that is being emitted from the heated, sunlit surface of 3I/ATLAS's nucleus, where ice sublimation occurs faster and thus ejects more dust.<ref name="Jewitt2025"/>{{rp|5}}<ref name="NASA-Hubble-Aug2025"/> The Sun-facing elongation of 3I/ATLAS's coma resembles those of other distant comets like [[C/2014 UN271 (Bernardinelli–Bernstein)|{{mp|C/2014 UN|271}} (Bernardinelli–Bernstein)]], which have been known to preferentially eject dust from the sunlit side of their surfaces.<ref name="Chandler2025"/>{{rp|24}}

By late August 2025, the coma of 3I/ATLAS no longer appeared elongated toward the Sun and the comet had developed an anti-solar tail.<ref name="ATel-17363"/><ref name="ATel-17372"/> However, the Sun-facing plume is still present, as telescope images from 26 August 2025 showed that the inner coma of 3I/ATLAS (within 5 arcseconds from the nucleus) appeared [[Hand fan|fan-shaped]] and slightly brighter on the Sun-facing side.<ref name="ATel-17372"/>

==== Tail ====
Hubble images from July 2025 first showed that 3I/ATLAS had a very faint and broad tail pointing eastward, in a direction away from the Sun.<ref name="Jewitt2025"/>{{rp|7}} A tail pointing away from the Sun is a common cometary feature that is formed when small dust particles are blown away by solar radiation pressure.<ref name="Jewitt2025"/>{{rp|5}} The broad appearance of this tail suggests that small dust particles were ejected from 3I/ATLAS's surface at high speeds.<ref name="Jewitt2025"/>{{rp|7}} The anti-solar tail of 3I/ATLAS was thought to be pointed directly away from Earth in July 2025, which would have made it [[foreshortening|foreshortened]] and mostly hidden behind 3I/ATLAS's coma.<ref name="Opitom2025"/>{{rp|2}}<ref name="Kareta2025"/>{{rp|2}} By the end of August 2025, observations by the 8.2-meter Gemini South telescope showed that the anti-solar tail of 3I/ATLAS had become more visible and had grown to 30 arcseconds in angular length or roughly {{cvt|56000|km|mi}}.<ref name="noirlab2525"/><ref name="ATel-17363"/>{{efn|name=Tail20250828|1=On 27.99 August 2025 the comet was 2.59 AU from Earth so the comet tail was roughly {{cvt|56000|km}} long. Math: 2.59 AU * (30/206265) = 56353 km}} The tail of 3I/ATLAS is expected to become more obvious as the comet approaches perihelion with changing viewing geometry and increasing cometary activity.<ref name="Opitom2025"/>{{rp|2}} As of 15 September, 3I/ATLAS had a visible dust tail length of 50 arcseconds (~100,000&nbsp;km).<ref name="ATel-17416"/> Post-perihelion, the tail of the comet was recovered by Michael Jäger on 8 November 2025.<ref>Michael Jäger (8 Nov 2025): [https://x.com/Komet123Jager/status/1987070482793853389 3I/ATLAS showed a complex tail structure early this morning]</ref>

The ESA in April 2026 reported that the gas/[[dust tail|tail]] of 3I/ATLAS stretches to the extent of 5 million kilometers away from the nucleus.<ref name="ESA20260402" /> These gas and dust emissions are relatively common in comets, and their dust tails can even extend to about 10 million kilometers from the nucleus.

The comet's Sun-facing plume (pointing right) is visible in all images. During August 2025 (bottom row), 3I/ATLAS begins to develop an anti-solar tail pointing left.<ref name="Gray2025"/>

=== Size and mass ===
High-resolution images by the Hubble Space Telescope from July 2025 indicate that the diameter of 3I/ATLAS's nucleus is between {{cvt|0.32 and 5.6|km|mi|1}}.<ref name="Jewitt2025"/><ref name="NASA-Hubble-Aug2025"/><ref name="ESA-Hubble-Aug2025"/> There is a large uncertainty in the estimated diameter of 3I/ATLAS's nucleus because it is surrounded by a coma of reflective dust, which makes the nucleus appear brighter and larger than it actually is.<ref name="Jewitt2025"/>{{rp|4, 12}} For example, early studies from July 2025 gave diameter estimates that were as high as {{cvt|10 to 20|km|mi}}, although astronomers were well aware that the nucleus of 3I/ATLAS should be much smaller.<ref name="Chandler2025"/><ref name="Seligman2025"/>{{rp|6}} While the exact brightness of the coma is unknown, Hubble images show that the coma's brightness must account for a large fraction of the nucleus's apparent brightness, so the actual diameter of 3I/ATLAS's nucleus should be at the lower end of the estimated range.<ref name="Jewitt2025"/>{{rp|4, 12}} The estimated dust loss rate of 3I/ATLAS suggests that its nucleus is likely less than a kilometer in diameter, like 2I/Borisov.<ref name="Jewitt2025"/>{{rp|11}}

Observations by various [[interplanetary spacecraft]] have shown that 3I/ATLAS experienced significant non-gravitational acceleration that peaked up to {{val|89.3|4.6|e=-9}}&nbsp;AU/day<sup>2</sup> one month before perihelion. If this non-gravitational acceleration is purely caused by outgassing, it would suggest that 3I/ATLAS's nucleus has a mass of roughly {{val|4.4|e=10|u=kg}}.<ref name="Eubanks2025-nongravs"/> If 3I/ATLAS has a typical comet nucleus density of {{val|200|-|600|u=kg/m3}}, then this mass would correspond to a nucleus diameter between {{cvt|0.520 and 0.748|km|mi|1}}, which is in agreement with estimates from Hubble imaging.<ref name="Eubanks2025-nongravs"/>

=== Composition and gas emissions ===
[[Near-infrared]] [[spectroscopy]] by JWST in August 2025 has shown that the coma of 3I/ATLAS is unusually rich in [[carbon dioxide]] ({{chem|CO|2}}) gas, with small amounts of water ice, water vapor, [[carbon monoxide]] (CO) gas, and [[carbonyl sulfide]] (OCS) gas.<ref name="Cordiner2025"/> The JWST has also revealed the presence of "heavy" {{chem|CO|2}} containing the [[isotope]] [[carbon-13]] (<sup>13</sup>C) in 3I/ATLAS's coma, although partial obscuration by dust and other gases makes it difficult to quantify the abundance of <sup>13</sup>C relative to the more common isotope [[carbon-12|<sup>12</sup>C]].<ref name="Cordiner2025"/> Spectroscopic observations by the [[SPHEREx]] [[space observatory]] agree that 3I/ATLAS contains high amounts of {{chem|CO|2}} in its coma, although SPHEREx did not have the sensitivity to detect water vapor and CO.<ref name="SPHEREx"/><ref name="BigThink-Aug2025"/>

From the August 2025 JWST observations, it is estimated that 3I/ATLAS's nucleus was emitting {{cvt|129 ± 1|kg|lbs}} of {{chem|CO|2}} per second,{{efn|name=CO2}} {{cvt|6.6 ± 0.2|kg|lbs|1}} of water per second,{{efn|name=H2O}} {{cvt|14.0 ± 0.9|kg|lbs|1}} of CO per second,{{efn|name=CO}} and {{cvt|0.43 ± 0.09|kg|lbs|2}} of OCS per second.{{efn|name=OCS}}<ref name="Cordiner2025"/> Analysis of [[absorption band|absorption features]] in JWST's spectrum of 3I/ATLAS suggests that the water ice in the comet's coma consists of fine grains smaller than 1&nbsp;micrometer in size.<ref name="Cordiner2025"/> The water ice in 3I/ATLAS is likely [[Phases of ice#Amorphous ice|amorphous]], although crystalline water ice cannot be ruled out.<ref name="Cordiner2025"/> A tentative detection of water vapor and [[hydroxyl radical]]s (OH) by the [[Swift Observatory]] on 31 July and 1 August 2025 suggested that the water ice grains in 3I/ATLAS's coma are sublimating beyond the nucleus,<ref name="Xing2025"/> likely at a distance between {{cvt|4000 and 10000|km|mi}} from the nucleus.<ref name="Cordiner2025"/> The water ice grains were most likely ejected from the comet's nucleus by outgassing of [[volatile (astrogeology)|volatile substances]] such as {{chem|CO|2}} and CO, rather than water ice sublimation.<ref name="Xing2025"/>

Mid-infared spectroscopy by JWST in December 2025 has added a novel detection of methane to the host of observed volatiles. The December 2025 re-visit of 3I/ATLAS shows an evolving production rate for the volatile species, both due to temporal evolution and a different heliocentric distance relative to the August observations.<ref name="belyakov etal" />

[[Ultraviolet spectroscopy]] by telescopes on Earth have additionally detected [[cyanide]] (CN) gas<ref name="ATel-17352"/> and atomic [[nickel]] (Ni I) vapor in the coma of 3I/ATLAS.<ref name="Rahatgaonkar2025"/>{{rp|1}} The emission of atomic nickel is not unusual; it has been seen in various comets, including the interstellar comet 2I/Borisov.<ref name="eso2108"/> However, no [[iron]] (Fe I) vapor was detected in 3I/ATLAS, which is unusual because nickel and iron are typically found in roughly equal amounts when outgassing from comets.<ref name="eso2108"/><ref name="Rahatgaonkar2025"/> Nickel emission in 3I/ATLAS was first detected by the Very Large Telescope (VLT) on 20 July 2025, and cyanide emission was first detected by the VLT later on 14 August 2025.<ref name="Rahatgaonkar2025"/>{{rp|5}} Throughout July to August 2025, the VLT observed a "rapid and steady" increase in the concentration of nickel and cyanide in 3I/ATLAS's coma, due to the comet's increasing activity during its approach to the Sun (from 4.4 to 2.85&nbsp;AU).<ref name="Rahatgaonkar2025"/>{{rp|7}} It is estimated that 3I/ATLAS was emitting {{cvt|4.6 ± 0.7|g|oz|2}} of nickel per second{{efn|name=Ni}} and {{cvt|17.6 ± 2.0|g|oz|2}} of cyanide per second by the time the VLT observations ended on 21 August 2025.{{efn|name=CN}}<ref name="Rahatgaonkar2025"/>{{rp|1}} Although it is unusual that nickel emission was detected before cyanide, the concentrations of nickel and cyanide in 3I/ATLAS are generally similar to those seen in other Solar System comets observed at similar distances from the Sun.<ref name="Rahatgaonkar2025"/>{{rp|9}} It is uncertain how nickel vapor is released from 3I/ATLAS; Rohan Rahatgaonkar and colleagues who analyzed the VLT observations proposed that there are several possible processes involving the [[chemical decomposition]] of nickel-containing [[organic compound]]s (e.g. [[nickel tetracarbonyl]]) via [[space weathering]].<ref name="Smithsonian-Aug2025"/><ref name="Rahatgaonkar2025"/>{{rp|12}} The amount of nickel observed in 3I/ATLAS is still consistent with earlier predictions that it should have a metal-poor composition.<ref name="Rahatgaonkar2025"/>{{rp|12}}

During July to August 2025, the VLT did not detect any signs of atomic [[oxygen]] [[Forbidden mechanism|[O I]]], [[dicarbon]] ({{chem|C|2}}), [[tricarbon]] ({{chem|C|3}}), and [[amino radical]]s ({{chem|NH|2}}) in the coma of 3I/ATLAS.<ref name="Rahatgaonkar2025"/>{{rp|12}} Likewise, observations by the [[MDM Observatory]] did not detect {{chem|C|2}} and {{chem|C|3}} in the coma of 3I/ATLAS during August 2025, which suggests that the comet is highly depleted in [[carbon chain]] compounds.<ref name="SalazarManzano2025"/> The upper limit to the comet's {{chem|C|2}}-to-CN ratio suggests that 3I/ATLAS is one of the most carbon chain-depleted comets ever known.<ref name="SalazarManzano2025"/>

<gallery mode="packed" heights="200" align="center">

The spectrum plots the brightness of 3I/ATLAS (vertical axis) over wavelength of light (horizontal axis). The gases that make up 3I/ATLAS ({{chem|H|2|O}}, {{chem|CO|2}}, and CO) can be seen as [[Emission spectrum|emission]] peaks, which are labeled with their respective names.<ref name="Cordiner2025"/>

==== Carbon dioxide abundance ====
[[File:3I comet CO2-H2O mixing ratios Cordiner et al. 2025 Fig 6.png|thumb|upright=1.5|Plot showing the [[carbon dioxide]]-to-water ({{chem|CO|2}}/{{chem|H|2|O}}) [[mixing ratio]]s of known comets (vertical axis) with distance from the Sun (horizontal axis). The dashed diagonal line highlights the trend of increasing {{chem|CO|2}}/{{chem|H|2|O}} mixing ratio with distance from the Sun. The two comets with anomalously high {{chem|CO|2}}/{{chem|H|2|O}} mixing ratios are labeled with red points: 3I/ATLAS (star) and [[C/2016 R2 (PanSTARRS)]] (circle).<ref name="Cordiner2025"/>]]

Within the coma of 3I/ATLAS, the [[mixing ratio]] of {{chem|CO|2}} relative to water is {{val|8.0|1.0}}—this is one of the highest {{chem|CO|2}} abundances seen in a comet, especially at its distance from the Sun (3.32&nbsp;AU) when it was first observed by JWST.<ref name="Cordiner2025"/> Whereas Solar System comets generally follow a trend of increasing {{chem|CO|2}}-to-water mixing ratio with distance from the Sun (due to {{chem|CO|2}} sublimating more than water at closer distances to the Sun),<ref name="BigThink-Aug2025"/> only 3I/ATLAS and the unusual Oort cloud comet [[C/2016 R2 (PanSTARRS)]] are known to break this trend with exceptionally high {{chem|CO|2}}-to-water mixing ratios.<ref name="Cordiner2025"/> On the other hand, the coma of 3I/ATLAS has a more typical CO-to-water mixing ratio of {{val|1.4|0.2}}, resembling other Solar System comets including the interstellar comet 2I/Borisov.<ref name="Cordiner2025"/>

The reason for the high abundance of {{chem|CO|2}} in 3I/ATLAS's coma is uncertain; this could either mean that the comet has a {{chem|CO|2}}-rich nucleus or there is some mechanism limiting the sublimation of water from its nucleus.<ref name="Cordiner2025"/> A team of NASA researchers led by [[Martin A. Cordiner]] have hypothesized that if 3I/ATLAS has a {{chem|CO|2}}-rich nucleus, the comet may have either been exposed to high amounts of [[irradiation|radiation]] or may have formed close to the {{chem|CO|2}} frost line in its parent star's protoplanetary disk.<ref name="Cordiner2025"/><ref name="SpaceCom-Aug2025"/> Alternatively, if 3I/ATLAS contains more water than suggested by JWST, 3I/ATLAS could have an unusually thick, insulating crust hiding water ice underneath.<ref name="Cordiner2025"/><ref name="SpaceCom-Aug2025"/> Further observations by the JWST, especially when 3I/ATLAS becomes more active, will be needed to determine which scenario is more likely.<ref name="Cordiner2025"/>

In April 2026, the [[European Space Agency|ESA]] released some more information about this interstellar comet. They have reported that 3I/ATLAS was emitting "70 Olympic Swimming Pools" worth of water vapor per day. More interesting is that they also reported that most of this water vapor was being emitted towards the sun. More reports of 3I/ATLAS will be released in due time once they gather more information from [[JUICE]].<ref name="ESA20260402" />

==== Silicate composition ====
[[File:Excerpt of Fig. 3 from Belyakov et al. 2026.png|thumb|359x359px|Plot showing the mid-infrared emissivity spectrum of 3I/ATLAS (red) compared to that of several Solar System comets (black). The locations of the spectral signatures of crystalline olivine are shown in green. 3I/ATLAS is an outlier from the ensemble of observed cometary mineralogies due to its lack of crystalline silicates.]]
[[Mid-infrared]] observations of 3I/ATLAS with the James Webb Space Telescope's [[Mid-Infrared Instrument]]'s Medium-Resolution Spectrometer have characterized the [[emissivity]] spectrum of the interstellar object.<ref name=":0">{{cite arXiv|last1=Belyakov |first1=Matthew |title=The Dust Mineralogy of Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS from JWST/MIRI Observations |date=25 June 2026 |eprint=2606.27535 |last2=Wong |first2=Ian |last3=Lisse |first3=Carey M. |last4=Davis |first4=M. Ryleigh |last5=Bolin |first5=Bryce T. |last6=Martin |first6=Audrey |last7=Pontoppidan |first7=Klaus M. |last8=Blake |first8=Geoffrey A. |last9=Chen |first9=Christine |class=astro-ph.EP }}</ref> Unlike all observed comets in the Solar System, 3I/ATLAS shows no evidence for crystalline silicates, and instead has a spectrum well-matched by amorphous silicates (of [[pyroxene]] and [[olivine]]-like stoichiometry), similar to those seen in the [[interstellar medium]] or evolved [[protoplanetary disk]]s. Comets in the Solar System show evidence for crystalline silicates due to turbulent radial mixing of condensed solids from the inner part of the disk outwards.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bockelée–Morvan |first1=D. |last2=Gautier |first2=D. |last3=Hersant |first3=F. |last4=Huré |first4=J.-M. |last5=Robert |first5=F. |date=1 March 2002 |title=Turbulent radial mixing in the solar nebula as the source of crystalline silicates in comets |url=https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/abs/2002/12/aa1967/aa1967.html |journal=Astronomy & Astrophysics |language=en |volume=384 |issue=3 |pages=1107–1118 |doi=10.1051/0004-6361:20020086 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2002A&A...384.1107B |issn=0004-6361}}</ref> The lack of such mineralogical components in 3I/ATLAS is additional evidence for a cold and distant formation out of material inherited from the interstellar medium.<ref name=":0" /> Additionally, 3I/ATLAS shows some evidence for the presence of carbonate minerals such as [[magnesite]] and [[siderite]], as well as abundant [[amorphous carbon]], which is a common solid-state constituent in comets.

=== Rotation ===
The nucleus of 3I/ATLAS is expected to be irregularly shaped like other comets, which should cause periodic variations in 3I/ATLAS's brightness as it rotates.<ref name="Chandler2025"/>{{rp|25}} However, because the nucleus of 3I/ATLAS is partially obscured by a dusty coma, the nucleus's brightness variations are reduced, which makes it difficult to measure its [[rotation period]] using telescopic observations.<ref name="Seligman2025"/>{{rp|8}}<ref name="Kareta2025"/>{{rp|4}}<ref name="Chandler2025"/>{{rp|5–6}} Some early studies from July 2025 were unable to determine a rotation period for 3I/ATLAS's nucleus,<ref name="Seligman2025"/><ref name="Feinstein2025"/><ref name="Chandler2025"/>{{rp|5}} but one study led by Raul de la Fuente Marcos and colleagues reported a rotation period of {{val|16.79|0.23}} hours, using observations by the Gran Telescopio Canarias from 2 to 5 July.<ref name="dela_Fuente_Marcos_2025"/> Another study published by Toni Santana-Ros and colleagues in August 2025 reported a similar (albeit shorter) rotation period of {{val|16.16|0.01}} hours, using observations by multiple different telescopes from 2 to 29 July.<ref name="Santana-Ros2025"/> Santana-Ros and colleagues noted that the brightness variations of 3I/ATLAS had decreased from 0.3 to 0.2 [[magnitude (astronomy)|magnitudes]] throughout July 2025, which likely indicates that 3I/ATLAS's nucleus became more obscured as it became more active.<ref name="Santana-Ros2025"/>{{rp|3}} In August 2025, Virginio Oldani and other Italian astronomers performed an analysis of 3I/ATLAS's coma shape in Hubble Space Telescope images and suggested that the rotational north pole of 3I/ATLAS's nucleus may be pointed toward the directions of either [[Right Ascension|RA]] 154°, [[Declination|Dec]] +25° or RA 334°, Dec –25°.<ref name="ATel-17350"/> A December 2025 analysis by Miquel Serra-Ricart and colleagues found that 3I/ATLAS exhibited a wobbling [[Comet#Jet|jet]] of gas and dust in images from August 2025, which they attribute to the rotation of the comet's nucleus.<ref name="Serra-Ricart2025"/> Serra-Ricart and colleagues determined a rotation period of {{val|15.48|0.70}} hours based on the wobbling rate of 3I/ATLAS jet.<ref name="Serra-Ricart2025"/>

== Exploration ==
A July 2025 study led by Atsuhiro Yaginuma and collaborators found that launching a [[space probe]] from Earth to perform a [[flyby (spaceflight)|fly by]] of 3I/ATLAS is not feasible, as any post-discovery launch (after 1 July 2025) would require an extremely high [[delta-v|delta-''v'']] (Δ''v'') at least {{val|24|u=km/s}}, which is beyond the capability of any [[propulsion system]] available at this time. If 3I/ATLAS had been discovered before 1 July 2025, a space probe launched from Earth on that date would have required Δ''v''~{{val|7|u=km/s}} to visit the comet. It would have been more feasible to visit 3I/ATLAS using a space probe departing from Mars, which requires substantially less Δ''v''. For example, putative space probes departing from Mars between July and September 2025 would require Δ''v''~{{val|5|u=km/s}} to fly by 3I/ATLAS in early October 2025.{{r|Yaginuma2025}}

[[File:ESA’s Mars and Jupiter missions observe comet 3I-ATLAS ESA512908.png|thumb|upright=1.3|Observability of 3I/ATLAS by ESA Mars and Jupiter spacecraft]]

Between 1 and 7 October 2025, two of ESA's Mars orbiters, [[Trace Gas Orbiter]] (TGO) and [[Mars Express]], observed 3I/ATLAS during its closest approach to the planet. TGO was able to capture the comet with its camera, but it couldn't be seen on photos by Mars Express, likely because of much lower exposure time.<ref name="ESA20251007"/> NASA's [[Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter]] also observed the comet, but data wasn't released due to NASA [[2025 United States federal government shutdown|being shut down]].{{r|NYT-20251007}} The [[China National Space Administration|CNSA]]'s Mars orbiter [[Tianwen-1]] also managed to image 3I/ATLAS.<ref name=WilliamsTianwen>{{cite news |last=Williams |first=Mathew |date=8 November 2025 |title=China's Tianwen-1 Orbiter Spots 3I/ATLAS|url=https://www.universetoday.com/articles/chinas-tianwen-1-orbiter-spots-3iatlas |work=Universe Today |publisher= Universe Today |access-date=8 November 2025}}</ref>

The [[Juno (spacecraft)|''Juno'']] spacecraft orbiting Jupiter may be able to observe 3I/ATLAS when it passes close to Jupiter in March 2026,{{r|Loeb2025-Juno}} but it is unlikely that ''Juno'' could be redirected to 3I/ATLAS because the spacecraft is low on fuel and has issues with its engine.{{r|NewSci-20250804}} Astrophysicist Marshall Eubanks has calculated that the ''[[Psyche (spacecraft)|Psyche]]'' spacecraft passed about {{convert|0.302|AU|e6km e6mi|abbr=unit}} from 3I/ATLAS on 4 September 2025, while the ''[[Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer]]'' (''Juice'') passed within {{convert|0.428|AU|e6km e6mi|abbr=unit}} from 3I/ATLAS on 4 November 2025.{{r|S&T-20250728|Eubanks_2025}} However, commanding these spacecraft to observe 3I/ATLAS would be difficult and could introduce risks to their primary missions.{{r|S&T-20250728}} Despite this, ''Juice'' observed 3I/ATLAS in November 2025 using its cameras, spectrometers, and a particle sensor.

From 30 October to 6 November 2025, it was predicted that [[Europa Clipper]] would potentially be immersed within the [[ion tail]] of 3I/ATLAS, providing the opportunity to detect the signatures of an interstellar comet's ion tail. Characteristic changes to the solar wind are also expected to be observed; a magnetic draping structure associated with the comet may be identifiable. It was further predicted that spacecraft ''[[Hera (spacecraft)|Hera]]'' would possibly be immersed within the ion tail of 3I/ATLAS from 25 October to 1 November 2025.{{r|Grant_2025}}

== Alien spacecraft speculation ==
On 16 July 2025, astrophysicist [[Avi Loeb]] and other researchers of the [[Initiative for Interstellar Studies]] posted a paper on [[arXiv]] speculating that 3I/ATLAS could be an [[Extraterrestrial UFO hypothesis|extraterrestrial spacecraft]] because they believed the object had "anomalous" characteristics,<ref name="Hibberd2025"/> such as having an apparently large size,<ref name="Loeb2025-size"/> lack of identifiable chemicals, and an apparently improbable trajectory aligned with the Solar System's [[ecliptic]] plane.<ref name="LiveScience-20250722"/> Other astronomers, including [[Chris Lintott]], immediately criticized Loeb's speculation; the science news website ''[[Live Science]]'' reported that "the overwhelming consensus is that it is a comet", with many researchers "disappointed with the new paper and pointed out that it distracts from the work of other scientists".<ref name="LiveScience-20250722"/> Several astrophysicists, including [[Scott Manley]] and [[David Kipping]], promptly pointed out flaws in Loeb's statistical analysis of 3I/ATLAS's trajectory.<ref name="Manley">{{cite AV media|title=Interstellar Comet 3/I ATLAS - Probably Isn't An Alien Spaceship|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MafmhXwPgmo|first=Scott|last=Manley|authorlink=Scott Manley|website=[[YouTube]]|date=4 August 2025|accessdate=23 August 2025}}</ref><ref name="Kipping">{{cite AV media|title=The Interstellar Object 3I/ATLAS, Avi Loeb and Aliens|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vFTHrdbeQYs|first=David|last=Kipping|authorlink=David Kipping|website=YouTube|date=23 August 2025|accessdate=23 August 2025}}</ref> [[Darryl Seligman]], who led the first published study on 3I/ATLAS, stated that "there have been numerous telescopic observations of 3I/ATLAS demonstrating that it's displaying classical signatures of cometary activity."<ref name="LiveScience-20250722"/> Seligman further elaborated that chemicals in 3I/ATLAS may not be detectable yet since the object was still far away from the Sun.<ref name="LiveScience-20250722"/> JWST has since confirmed that 3I/ATLAS is outgassing {{chem|CO|2}}, water, and CO.<ref name="Cordiner2025"/><ref name="BigThink-Aug2025"/>
On 31 July to 1 August, the [[Swift Observatory]] found tentative evidence for water vapor and OH. Cyanide gas (CN) and atomic nickel vapor were detected by the VLT on 14 August 2025 and 20 July 2025 respectively.<ref name="Rahatgaonkar2025"/>{{rp|1}} These substances are commonly found in comets.<ref name="eso2108"/>

Loeb [[Avi Loeb#'Oumuamua|previously suggested]] that [[1I/{{okina}}Oumuamua]] and other interstellar objects including the possibly interstellar [[meteor]] [[CNEOS 2014-01-08]] could be extraterrestrial spacecraft, for which he was also criticized by many researchers.<ref name="LiveScience-20250722"/><ref name="CT-20190204">{{cite news |last=Groll |first=Johan |title=Thinking About Distant Civilizations Isn't Speculative |url=http://www.spiegel.de/international/zeitgeist/astronomer-avi-loeb-on-the-interstellar-body-oumuamua-a-1246803.html |date=7 January 2019 |work=[[Der Spiegel]] |access-date=7 January 2019 }}</ref> While Loeb has written in his blog that "the most likely outcome will be that 3I/ATLAS is a completely natural interstellar object, probably a comet," he defended his hypothesis as an "interesting exercise in its own right, and is fun to explore, irrespective of its likely validity".<ref name="LiveScience-20250722"/> Astronomer [[Samantha Lawler]] highlighted that "while it is important to remain open-minded about any 'testable prediction', the new paper [by Loeb et al.] pushes this sentiment to the limit."<ref name="LiveScience-20250722"/> Lawler further said that [[extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence]], while "the evidence presented [by Loeb et al.] is absolutely not extraordinary."<ref name="LiveScience-20250722"/>

== Notes ==
{{Notelist|notes=

{{efn|name=CO2|[[Carbon dioxide]] or {{chem|CO|2}} has a [[molar mass]] of 44.009 grams/[[mole (unit)|mole]], where 1&nbsp;mole is equivalent to {{val|6.022|e=23}} molecules ([[Avogadro's number]]). The "whole-coma equivalent" {{chem|CO|2}} emission rate of {{val|1.76|0.02|e=27}} {{chem|CO|2}} molecules/second given in Cordiner et al. (2025) can be divided by {{val|6.022|e=23}} molecules/mole to give ≈2923&nbsp;moles of {{chem|CO|2}}/second. Dividing the moles of {{chem|CO|2}} by the molar mass of {{chem|CO|2}} gives a {{chem|CO|2}} mass emission rate of ≈{{val|1.286|e=4}}&nbsp;grams/second, or ≈128.6&nbsp;kilograms/second when multiplying by 1 kilogram/1000 gram. Rounding the result down to the appropriate number of [[significant figures]] gives ≈129 kilograms/second. The uncertainty is calculated via [[propagation of error]].}}

{{efn|name=H2O|[[Water]] or {{chem|H|2|O}} has a [[molar mass]] of 18.015 grams/[[mole (unit)|mole]], where 1&nbsp;mole is equivalent to {{val|6.022|e=23}} molecules ([[Avogadro's number]]). The "whole-coma equivalent" {{chem|H|2|O}} emission rate of {{val|2.19|0.08|e=26}} {{chem|H|2|O}} molecules/second given in Cordiner et al. (2025) can be divided by {{val|6.022|e=23}} molecules/mole to give ≈363.7&nbsp;moles of {{chem|H|2|O}}/second. Dividing the moles of {{chem|H|2|O}} by the molar mass of {{chem|H|2|O}} gives a {{chem|H|2|O}} mass emission rate of ≈{{val|6.552|e=3}}&nbsp;grams/second, or ≈6.552&nbsp;kilograms/second when multiplying by 1 kilogram/1000 gram. Rounding the result down to the appropriate number of [[significant figures]] gives ≈6.55 kilograms/second. The uncertainty is calculated via [[propagation of error]].}}

{{efn|name=CO|[[Carbon monoxide]] or CO has a [[molar mass]] of 28.010 grams/[[mole (unit)|mole]], where 1&nbsp;mole is equivalent to {{val|6.022|e=23}} molecules ([[Avogadro's number]]). The "whole-coma equivalent" CO emission rate of {{val|3.0|0.2|e=26}} CO molecules/second given in Cordiner et al. (2025) can be divided by {{val|6.022|e=23}} molecules/mole to give ≈498.2&nbsp;moles of CO/second. Dividing the moles of CO by the molar mass of CO gives a CO mass emission rate of ≈{{val|1.395|e=4}}&nbsp;grams/second, or ≈13.95&nbsp;kilograms/second when multiplying by 1 kilogram/1000 gram. Rounding the result down to the appropriate number of [[significant figures]] gives ≈14.0 kilograms/second. The uncertainty is calculated via [[propagation of error]].}}

{{efn|name=OCS|[[Carbonyl sulfide]] or OCS has a [[molar mass]] of 60.075 grams/[[mole (unit)|mole]], where 1&nbsp;mole is equivalent to {{val|6.022|e=23}} molecules ([[Avogadro's number]]). The "whole-coma equivalent" CO emission rate of {{val|4.3|0.9|e=24}} OCS molecules/second given in Cordiner et al. (2025) can be divided by {{val|6.022|e=23}} molecules/mole to give ≈7.140&nbsp;moles of OCS/second. Dividing the moles of OCS by the molar mass of OCS gives a OCS mass emission rate of ≈{{val|429.0}}&nbsp;grams/second, or ≈0.4290&nbsp;kilograms/second when multiplying by 1 kilogram/1000 gram. Rounding the result down to the appropriate number of [[significant figures]] gives ≈0.43 kilograms/second. The uncertainty is calculated via [[propagation of error]].}}

{{efn|name=Ni|Atomic [[nickel]] (Ni) has an average [[molar mass]] of 58.693 grams/[[mole (unit)|mole]], where 1&nbsp;mole is equivalent to {{val|6.022|e=23}} molecules ([[Avogadro's number]]). Rahatgaonkar et al. (2025) give a [[logarithm]]ic emission rate of {{val|22.67|0.07}}, which can be plugged in as an exponent of 10 to give the actual Ni emission rate of 10<sup>22.67</sup>&nbsp;≈&nbsp;{{val|3.981|e=22}} Ni atoms/second. The actual Ni emission rate can then be divided by {{val|6.022|e=23}} molecules/mole to give ≈0.0661&nbsp;moles of Ni/second. Dividing the moles of Ni by the molar mass of Ni gives a Ni mass emission rate of ≈{{val|4.559}}&nbsp;grams/second. Rounding the result down to the appropriate number of [[significant figures]] gives ≈4.6 grams/second. The uncertainty is calculated via [[propagation of error]].}}

{{efn|name=CN|[[Cyanide]] or CN has a [[molar mass]] of 26.018 grams/[[mole (unit)|mole]], where 1&nbsp;mole is equivalent to {{val|6.022|e=23}} molecules ([[Avogadro's number]]). Rahatgaonkar et al. (2025) give a [[logarithm]]ic emission rate of {{val|23.61|0.05}}, which can be plugged in as an exponent of 10 to give the actual CN emission rate of 10<sup>23.61</sup>&nbsp;≈&nbsp;{{val|4.571|e=23}} CN molecules/second. The actual CN emission rate can then be divided by {{val|6.022|e=23}} molecules/mole to give ≈0.7590&nbsp;moles of CN/second. Dividing the moles of CN by the molar mass of CN gives a CN mass emission rate of ≈{{val|17.60}}&nbsp;grams/second. Rounding the result down to the appropriate number of [[significant figures]] gives ≈17.6 grams/second. The uncertainty is calculated via [[propagation of error]].}}

{{efn|name=n-body|An [[n-body problem|n-body integration]] shows 3I/ATLAS came to [[Apsis#Time of perihelion|perihelion]] about 7 minutes before the [[two-body problem|two-body]] [[JPL SBDB]] epoch 19 February 2026 solution. (Changing JPL SBDB 11:52 to Horizons 11:45.) The comet also passed {{convert|0.00003|AU|e3km e3mi|abbr=unit}} closer to the Sun. (Math: 1.356 481 "JPL SBDB" − 1.356 448 "Horizons" {{=}} 0.000 03)}}

}}
